```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(broom)
library(gt)

# Site tokens (see custom.scss / DESIGN_SYSTEM.md)
sage  <- "#5C715E"  # $accent
sage2 <- "#8FAF9E"  # $accent2
sage3 <- "#A7C7B5"  # $accent3
ink   <- "#2F3E46"  # $body-color
hot   <- "#B5483B"  # "look here" highlight
amber <- "#E8A33D"
grp_cols <- c(sage2, amber)

theme_deck <- function(base_size = 22) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      axis.title = element_text(color = ink),
      axis.text = element_text(color = ink),
      plot.title = element_text(color = ink, face = "bold"),
      legend.text = element_text(color = ink),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

# Formatting helpers so every number on a slide comes from the data.
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
fp <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p))))

# Welch independent-samples t-test summary (first factor level minus second);
# d uses the pooled SD.
ind_stats <- function(y, g) {
  g <- factor(g); lv <- levels(g)
  a <- y[g == lv[1]]; b <- y[g == lv[2]]
  tt <- t.test(x = a, y = b, var.equal = FALSE)
  sp <- sqrt(((length(a) - 1) * var(a) + (length(b) - 1) * var(b)) /
               (length(a) + length(b) - 2))
  list(lv = lv, n1 = length(a), n2 = length(b), m1 = mean(a), m2 = mean(b),
       s1 = sd(a), s2 = sd(b), sp = sp, diff = mean(a) - mean(b),
       t = unname(tt$statistic), df = unname(tt$parameter), p = tt$p.value,
       ci = tt$conf.int, d = (mean(a) - mean(b)) / sp)
}
fdf <- function(df) ifelse(abs(df - round(df)) < 1e-6, as.character(round(df)), f2(df))
apa_t <- function(r) sprintf("t(%s) = %s, p %s", fdf(r$df), f2(r$t), fp(r$p))

# ---- Example datasets -------------------------------------------------
# Coffee vs. decaf happiness (built to have exactly these means and SDs)
set.seed(11)
exact <- function(n, m, sd) m + sd * scale(rnorm(n))[, 1]
coffee <- tibble(
  grp = factor(rep(c("Experimental", "Control"), each = 10),
               levels = c("Experimental", "Control")),
  happy = c(exact(10, 8, 1), exact(10, 6, 1))
)
cf <- ind_stats(coffee$happy, coffee$grp)

# Chocolate and concentration (0-20 scale)
set.seed(42)
choco <- data.frame(
  concentration = c(rnorm(25, 15, 2), rnorm(25, 13.5, 2)),
  group = factor(rep(c("chocolate", "no_chocolate"), each = 25),
                 levels = c("chocolate", "no_chocolate"))
)
ch <- ind_stats(choco$concentration, choco$group)

# Music and studying (0-10 quiz)
set.seed(99)
music <- data.frame(
  quiz_score = c(rnorm(20, 8, 1), rnorm(20, 7, 1.2)) |> pmin(10),
  group = factor(rep(c("music", "silence"), each = 20),
                 levels = c("music", "silence"))
)
mu_ <- ind_stats(music$quiz_score, music$group)

# Phone use and sleep quality (1-10 scale)
set.seed(77)
sleep <- data.frame(
  sleep_quality = c(rnorm(40, 6.8, 1), rnorm(40, 7.4, 0.9)),
  group = factor(rep(c("phone", "no_phone"), each = 40),
                 levels = c("no_phone", "phone"))
)
sl <- ind_stats(sleep$sleep_quality, sleep$group)

# Practice datasets
set.seed(103)
ex_3 <- tibble(
  Group = factor(rep(c("Caffeine", "Placebo"), each = 20),
                 levels = c("Caffeine", "Placebo")),
  Alertness = c(rnorm(20, mean = 75, sd = 8), rnorm(20, mean = 68, sd = 8))
)
set.seed(104)
ex_4 <- tibble(
  Format = factor(rep(c("Online", "InPerson"), each = 25),
                  levels = c("Online", "InPerson")),
  Exam_Score = c(rnorm(25, mean = 82, sd = 5), rnorm(25, mean = 79, sd = 6))
)
e3 <- ind_stats(ex_3$Alertness, ex_3$Group)
e4 <- ind_stats(ex_4$Exam_Score, ex_4$Format)

# A reusable results plot for each worked example
group_plot <- function(d, x, y, ylab, title, kind = "box") {
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(.data[[x]], .data[[y]], fill = .data[[x]]))
  p <- switch(kind,
    box = p + geom_boxplot(alpha = .6, outlier.shape = NA),
    violin = p + geom_violin(alpha = .5, trim = FALSE),
    bar = p + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "col", width = .5, alpha = .8))
  p +
    geom_jitter(width = .12, alpha = .5, size = 2, color = ink) +
    stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = .2, color = ink) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = grp_cols) +
    labs(title = title, y = ylab, x = NULL) +
    theme_deck(20)
}

# Results table for a worked example
results_tbl <- function(r) {
  tibble(
    Difference = r$diff, t = r$t, df = fdf(r$df),
    p = ifelse(r$p < .001, "<.001", sprintf("%.3f", r$p)),
    `CI[ll,uu]` = paste0("[", f2(r$ci[1]), ", ", f2(r$ci[2]), "]"),
    d = r$d
  ) |>
    gt() |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Difference, t, d), decimals = 2) |>
    opt_row_striping() |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = 22, table.width = pct(100)) |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
              locations = cells_column_labels())
}
```

## From Paired to Independent Samples

Last time, we compared **two related means**: the *same participants* measured twice (e.g., stress before vs. after a mindfulness program).

Now, we'll compare **two unrelated means**: *different participants* in each group.

| Paired t-test                          | Independent t-test             |
|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Same people                            | Different people               |
| Within-subjects                        | Between-subjects               |
| Reduces error (individual differences) | Must estimate error separately |

## From Paired to Independent Samples

### Visual comparison

```{r}
#| label: from-paired-to-independent-samples
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
library(patchwork)
set.seed(5)
paired <- tibble(
  condition = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Post"), each = 10), levels = c("Pre", "Post")),
  id = rep(1:10, 2)
) |> mutate(score = c(rnorm(10, 70, 5)) |> (\(x) c(x, x + 5 + rnorm(10, 0, 2)))())
independent <- tibble(
  group = rep(c("Control", "Experimental"), each = 10),
  score = c(rnorm(10, 70, 5), rnorm(10, 75, 5))
)

p1 <- ggplot(paired, aes(condition, score, group = id)) +
  geom_line(color = sage3, linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(color = sage, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Paired: same people", y = "Score", x = NULL) +
  theme_deck(20)

p2 <- ggplot(independent, aes(group, score, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = .1, color = ink, alpha = .6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = grp_cols) +
  labs(title = "Independent: different people", y = "Score", x = NULL) +
  theme_deck(20)

p1 + p2
```

## Sampling Theory (Recap)

### Comparing two unrelated groups

- Sampling theory lets us test two unrelated groups.

- Under $H_0$ the **difference** between group means is centered on 0. Under $H_A$ it is centered somewhere else.

```{r}
#| label: sampling-theory-recap
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.8
rec_dat <- tibble(
  x = rep(seq(-5, 6, length.out = 400), 2),
  y = c(dnorm(seq(-5, 6, length.out = 400), 0, 1),
        dnorm(seq(-5, 6, length.out = 400), 2, 1)),
  hypothesis = factor(rep(c("Null hypothesis", "Alternative hypothesis"), each = 400),
                      levels = c("Null hypothesis", "Alternative hypothesis"))
)
rec_plot <- ggplot(rec_dat, aes(x, y, color = hypothesis, linetype = hypothesis)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(sage, ink)) +
  labs(x = "Difference between the group means (in standard errors)", y = NULL,
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_deck(20) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
rec_plot
```

## Sampling Theory (Recap)

### A difference near 0 looks like the null

```{r}
#| label: sampling-theory-recap-2
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.8
rec_plot + geom_vline(xintercept = -.8, color = hot, linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("text", x = -.8, y = .42, label = "observed", color = hot, hjust = 1.1, size = 6)
```

- An observed difference like this is easy to produce when $H_0$ is true.

## Sampling Theory (Recap)

### A difference beyond the critical value does not

```{r}
#| label: sampling-theory-recap-3
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.8
rec_plot +
  geom_vline(xintercept = qnorm(.95), color = ink, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = qnorm(.95), y = .42, label = "critical value",
           color = ink, hjust = -.1, size = 6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2.2, color = hot, linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.2, y = .3, label = "observed", color = hot, hjust = -.15, size = 6)
```

- Beyond the critical value, the observed difference would be very unusual under $H_0$, so we **reject** it.

## Inferential Statistics

### Applied to independent groups

- Our goal is still to test whether a difference is likely due to chance.

- With independent samples, chance variation now includes **differences between individuals** in *both* groups.

## Group Variance

### Within and between

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
To compare the means we need to know:

- **Between-group variance:** how much the answers from the **experimental** group differ from the **control** group.

- **Within-group variance:** how much scores differ from one another **inside** each group, around that group's own mean.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: group-variance
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.4
set.seed(3)
gv <- tibble(
  treatment = factor(rep(c("Experimental", "Control"), each = 30),
                     levels = c("Experimental", "Control")),
  score = c(rnorm(30, 30, 4), rnorm(30, 38, 4))
)
ggplot(gv, aes(treatment, score, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = .35, width = .8, color = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = .1, alpha = .5, size = 2, color = ink) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 5, color = hot) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = grp_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Score", subtitle = "red dot = group mean") +
  theme_deck(20)
```
:::
:::::

## Signal and Noise

### Same difference, different spread

```{r}
#| label: signal-and-noise
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
sn <- function(sd_, lab) {
  d <- tibble(
    grp = factor(rep(c("Group 1", "Group 2"), each = 10)),
    y = c(exact(10, 8, sd_), exact(10, 6, sd_)), panel = lab)
  list(d = d, r = ind_stats(d$y, d$grp))
}
lo <- sn(1, "Little spread (SD = 1)")
hi <- sn(3, "Lots of spread (SD = 3)")
set.seed(8)
ggplot(bind_rows(lo$d, hi$d) |> mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = unique(panel))),
       aes(grp, y, fill = grp)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = .12, size = 2, color = ink, alpha = .7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = grp_cols) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Score") +
  theme_deck(20)
```

## Signal and Noise

### t is signal divided by noise

$$t = \frac{\text{signal}}{\text{noise}} = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{SE}$$

- In the previous slide, both panels have the **same** mean difference ($8 - 6 = 2$), so the same signal.

- Little spread: $t = `r f2(lo$r$t)`$. Lots of spread: $t = `r f2(hi$r$t)`$. More noise means a smaller $t$, so a difference is harder to trust.

## Introduction to Independent-Samples t-Test

### What is an independent-samples t-test?

::: hero-def
[Independent-Samples t-Test]{.term-pill}

: A statistical method for comparing the means of **two unrelated** groups, such as different people randomly assigned to two conditions.
:::

## Independent-Samples t-Test Overview

Used when we compare **two different groups** on a continuous outcome.

:::::: badge-row
::: content-badge
[local_cafe]{.material-icons}

#### Coffee vs. decaf

Happiness scores
:::

::: content-badge
[headphones]{.material-icons}

#### Music vs. silence

Study performance
:::

::: content-badge
[smartphone]{.material-icons}

#### Phone vs. no phone

Sleep quality before bed
:::
::::::

- **Goal:** is the mean difference between groups larger than what we'd expect by chance?

## Independent-Samples t-Test

### Example

> The experimental group drinks caffeinated coffee. The control group drinks decaf. I ask both groups to complete a survey to measure their happiness on a scale of `1` to `10`.

- The experimental group has a mean happiness score of `8`.

- The control group has a mean happiness score of `6`.

::: fragment
Is the group that drank coffee significantly happier than the control group?
:::

## A New Sampling Distribution

### The difference between two sample means

- In the one-sample test we asked how far a sample mean falls from $\mu$.

- Now there are **two** sample means, so the thing that bounces around from study to study is their **difference**, $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$.

- If $H_0$ is true (both groups come from populations with the same mean), those differences pile up around **0**. The test asks how far from 0 ours landed, in standard-error units.

## Let's Watch It Happen

### Simulating 5000 studies

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
sampling_difference.R

```{r}
#| label: sampling-difference
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
set.seed(seed = 11)
sigma <- 1      # both populations have the same SD
n     <- 10     # people per group

# Run the "study" 5000 times with H0 true (same mean, 7, in both groups)
diffs <- replicate(n = 5000, expr = {
  group_1 <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 7, sd = sigma)
  group_2 <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 7, sd = sigma)
  mean(x = group_1) - mean(x = group_2)
})

c(simulated_sd = sd(x = diffs),
  formula = sigma * sqrt(x = 1 / n + 1 / n))
```
:::

- The spread of the simulated differences **is** the standard error of the difference, and the formula $\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}$ predicts it.

## A New Sampling Distribution

### What the 5000 differences look like

```{r}
#| label: plot-sampling-difference
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(tibble(d = diffs), aes(d)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, fill = sage3, color = "white") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = sigma * sqrt(2 / n)),
                color = hot, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = ink) +
  labs(x = "Difference between the two sample means", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "red curve = normal with mean 0 and SD = the standard error of the difference") +
  theme_deck(20) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

## Why the Standard Errors Add

### From one mean to a difference of two

$$SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad SE_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma^2}{n_2}} = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}$$

- Each sample mean has its own wobble, $\sigma^2/n_j$ (the squared standard error).

- A difference inherits the wobble of **both** means, and variances **add** (even when you subtract), so the two squared standard errors add. Then we take the square root.

- Two noisy means make a noisier difference than either one alone. That is why this denominator is bigger than the one-sample $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

## Formulas

### Theoretical and computational

Inferential statistics have both **theoretical** and **computational** formulas:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Theoretical

The formula if we actually knew the population parameters ($\sigma$).
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Computational

The formula for estimating the test statistic based solely on sample data.
:::
:::
:::::

## Theoretical Formula

### If we knew the population standard deviation

$$z = \frac{\color{#B5483B}{\bar{x}_1} - \color{#5C715E}{\bar{x}_2}}{\color{#2F3E46}{\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}}$$

- The numerator is really $(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)$. Under $H_0$ the second part is $0$, so it drops out.

- [Sample mean, group 1]{style="color:#B5483B"}

- [Sample mean, group 2]{style="color:#5C715E"}

- [Standard error of the difference]{style="color:#2F3E46"}, using the population $\sigma$ (assumed equal in both groups)

## Computational Formula

### Estimating from the samples (pooled t-test)

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\color{#5C715E}{s_p^2}\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}} \qquad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$$

- [$s_p^2$ = pooled variance]{style="color:#5C715E"}, a weighted average of the two group variances.

- $df = n_1 + n_2 - 2$

## Computational Formula

### When the variances are not equal (Welch's t-test)

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}$$

- No pooling: each group's variance keeps its own weight, and df is adjusted (it is usually not a whole number). Each $s_j^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2}{n_j - 1}$ is that group's own variance: squared distances from its own mean, divided by $n_j - 1$.

- This is what `t.test()` does **by default** in R. Adding `var.equal = TRUE` gives the pooled version above.

## Pooled or Welch: Same Idea

### Both add the two squared standard errors

$$\text{Welch: } \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} \qquad\qquad \text{Pooled: } \sqrt{\frac{s_p^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_p^2}{n_2}}, \quad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$$

- Welch lets each group keep its **own** variance. Pooling uses one shared $s_p^2$, a **weighted average** (bigger groups count more).

- With equal $n$ and similar variances the two agree (coffee: identical $t$).

- When variances differ a lot, $s_p^2$ stops describing either group. Next: what goes wrong.

## Where df Comes From

### Two means estimated, two degrees lost

- The pooled $s_p^2$ uses **two** sample means (one per group) to measure spread.

- Each estimated mean costs one degree of freedom: $(n_1 - 1) + (n_2 - 1) = n_1 + n_2 - 2$.

- Coffee: $10 + 10 - 2 = 18$. Welch adjusts df to account for unequal variances, so it is usually not a whole number.

## Coffee Example

### Manual

::: callout-tip
## Pooled variance and standard error

$s_p^2 = \dfrac{(10-1)(1)^2 + (10-1)(1)^2}{10 + 10 - 2} = `r f2(cf$sp^2)`$ and $SE = \sqrt{`r f2(cf$sp^2)`\left(\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10}\right)} = `r f2(sqrt(cf$sp^2 * (1/cf$n1 + 1/cf$n2)))`$
:::

::: callout-tip
## Compute t

$t = \dfrac{8 - 6}{`r f2(sqrt(cf$sp^2 * (1/cf$n1 + 1/cf$n2)))`} = `r f2(cf$t)`$

The denominator is $SE = \sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}$, the standard error of the difference between the two means.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Decide

$df = 10 + 10 - 2 = `r cf$df`$. At $\alpha = .05$ (two-tailed), $t_{critical} = \pm `r f3(qt(.975, cf$df))`$. Since $`r f2(cf$t)` > `r f3(qt(.975, cf$df))`$, we **reject** $H_0$.
:::

## Coffee Example

### Data overview

```{r}
#| label: coffee-example
#| echo: false
t.test(formula = happy ~ grp, data = coffee) |>
  tidy() |>
  rename(mdiff = estimate, t = statistic, Experimental = estimate1,
         Control = estimate2, df = parameter) |>
  mutate(`CI[ll,uu]` = paste0("[", round(conf.low, 2), ", ", round(conf.high, 2), "]"),
         p = ifelse(p.value < .001, "<.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))) |>
  select(mdiff, t, df, p, Experimental, Control, `CI[ll,uu]`) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mdiff, t, Experimental, Control), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = df, decimals = 2, drop_trailing_zeros = TRUE) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = 30, table.width = pct(80)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels())
```

- `mdiff` is the experimental mean minus the control mean ($8 - 6 = 2$). The factor levels set the order, so put the group you want **first** to get a positive difference.

## Reading the `t.test()` Output

### Every piece comes from the formula

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
coffee_t_test.R

```{r}
#| label: coffee-t-test-output
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
t.test(formula = happy ~ grp, data = coffee)   # Welch by default
```
:::

## Reading the `t.test()` Output

### Where each number comes from

- **`t`** $= \dfrac{\text{mean difference}}{SE} = \dfrac{8 - 6}{`r f2(sqrt(cf$sp^2 * (1/cf$n1 + 1/cf$n2)))`} = `r f2(cf$t)`$. The two **means** are listed at the bottom, the standard error is never printed.

- **`df`** is computed from the two variances (Welch). Here it equals $n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 18$ because the groups match in size and spread. **`p-value`** is the area beyond $\pm t$ in both tails of that $t$ distribution.

- **95% CI** is the mean difference $\pm\ t_{critical} \times SE$, an interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$.

## Independent-Samples t-Test

### Assumptions

::: callout-important
## Assumptions

1.  **DV is continuous** (interval or ratio scale).
2.  **Observations are independent**, and the data are randomly sampled. Each person appears in only one group.
3.  **Normality:** each group's distribution is approximately normal (or the groups are large enough for the CLT).
4.  **Equal variances (homogeneity of variance):** the two groups have similar spread. Only the **pooled** test needs this.
:::

## Why Equal Variances?

### The pooled test uses one shared variance

- Pooling says: "both groups are estimating the **same** $\sigma^2$, so combine them into one $s_p^2$."

- That is only a fair summary when the groups really do have similar spread.

- Say a small group is very noisy ($n = 10$, $s = 4$) and a large group is steady ($n = 40$, $s = 1$):

```{r}
#| label: pooled-vs-welch-se
#| echo: false
n1_ <- 10; s1_ <- 4; n2_ <- 40; s2_ <- 1
sp2_ <- ((n1_ - 1) * s1_^2 + (n2_ - 1) * s2_^2) / (n1_ + n2_ - 2)
se_pooled_ <- sqrt(sp2_ * (1 / n1_ + 1 / n2_))
se_welch_  <- sqrt(s1_^2 / n1_ + s2_^2 / n2_)
```

$$SE_{pooled} = `r f2(se_pooled_)` \qquad SE_{Welch} = \sqrt{\tfrac{4^2}{10} + \tfrac{1^2}{40}} = `r f2(se_welch_)`$$

- The pooled version leans on the big, quiet group and **understates** the noise. A standard error that is too small makes $t$ too big.

## What Goes Wrong

### Simulating false alarms

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
false_alarms.R

```{r}
#| label: false-alarms
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
set.seed(seed = 348)

# Two groups with the SAME true mean (H0 is true). How often is p < .05?
one_study <- function(n1, sd1, n2, sd2) {
  x <- rnorm(n = n1, mean = 0, sd = sd1)
  y <- rnorm(n = n2, mean = 0, sd = sd2)
  c(pooled = t.test(x = x, y = y, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value,
    welch  = t.test(x = x, y = y, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value)
}

unequal <- replicate(n = 4000, expr = one_study(n1 = 10, sd1 = 4, n2 = 40, sd2 = 1))
equal   <- replicate(n = 4000, expr = one_study(n1 = 25, sd1 = 2, n2 = 25, sd2 = 2))

rbind(unequal_groups = rowMeans(x = unequal < .05),
      equal_groups   = rowMeans(x = equal < .05))
```
:::

## What Goes Wrong

### The false-alarm rate

- We want about **.05**. With unequal spread and unequal $n$, the pooled test cries wolf **`r round(100 * mean(unequal["pooled", ] < .05))`%** of the time. Welch stays near 5%.

- That is why we check: the pooled test is only trustworthy when the spreads are similar.

## Checking Equal Variances

### Look first, then test

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
compare_spread.R

```{r}
#| label: compare-spread
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
aggregate(x = concentration ~ group, data = choco, FUN = sd)
```
:::

- **Look:** are the group SDs in the same ballpark? A rough rule is that the largest SD is no more than about twice the smallest.

- **Test:** **Levene's Test** asks the same question formally. $H_0$: the group variances are equal.

## Levene's Test in R

### One row of results, not two

```{r}
#| label: levene-intro-data
#| echo: false
set.seed(24)
noisy <- tibble(
  group = factor(rep(c("small_noisy", "large_steady"), times = c(10, 40))),
  score = c(rnorm(10, 0, 4), rnorm(40, 0, 1))
)
```

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
levene_intro.R

```{r}
#| label: levene-intro
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
library(car)
leveneTest(y = score ~ group, data = noisy)
```
:::

- R prints **one** row of results. There are no "top row / bottom row" versions to choose from. Read the `Pr(>F)` column: that is the $p$-value.

- $p < .05$: the variances **differ**, so do not trust the pooled test. $p > .05$: no evidence they differ.

## What R Does Instead of Two Rows

### Choosing with `var.equal`

- SPSS prints a "pooled" row and a "Welch" row. In R you **choose with one argument**:

  - `var.equal = FALSE` (the **default**): Welch, no equal-variance assumption

  - `var.equal = TRUE`: pooled, needs equal variances

- Traditional route: run Levene's Test, then pick (pooled if $p > .05$, Welch if $p < .05$).

- Many statisticians now **always use Welch**: nearly identical when variances are equal, protective when they are not.

- Here, we check Levene's Test to see whether pooling was safe, then run **Welch** anyway.

## Looking Ahead: Sphericity

### The same idea in repeated measures

::: callout-tip
## The same idea comes back

Here the assumption is **equal variances across groups**. In a repeated-measures design with three or more conditions, the matching assumption is **sphericity**: the *difference scores* between every pair of conditions have similar variance.

The paired $t$-test never needed it, because two conditions give only **one** set of differences.
:::

## Let's Apply It

### Three independent designs

We'll test three common between-subjects designs:

:::::: badge-row
::: content-badge
[cookie]{.material-icons}

#### Chocolate and Concentration

Experimental vs. control

::: content-badge
[headphones]{.material-icons}

Environmental manipulation

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Design

> 50 undergraduate students from XYZ University were randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group received a small piece of chocolate (70% dark cocoa) to consume before completing a 10-minute concentration task. The other group received no chocolate. The task measured sustained attention and was scored on a 0-20 scale.

- **IV:** chocolate (yes vs. no)

- **DV:** concentration task score

- **Design:** between-subjects, randomized

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Hypotheses

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Null hypothesis $H_0$

Concentration is the same with and without chocolate.

$\mu_\text{chocolate} = \mu_\text{no chocolate}$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Alternative hypothesis $H_A$

Concentration differs between the groups.

$\mu_\text{chocolate} \neq \mu_\text{no chocolate}$
:::
:::
:::::

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Data and results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: does-chocolate-improve-concentration
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
group_plot(choco, "group", "concentration", "Concentration score",
           "Chocolate and concentration")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: does-chocolate-improve-concentration-2
#| echo: false
results_tbl(ch)
```

Chocolate: $M = `r f2(ch$m1)`$, $SD = `r f2(ch$s1)`$. No chocolate: $M = `r f2(ch$m2)`$, $SD = `r f2(ch$s2)`$.
:::
:::::

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Check the assumption

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
levene.R

```{r}
#| label: levene
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
library(car)

# Equal variances? (H0: the variances are equal)
leveneTest(y = concentration ~ group, data = choco)
```
:::

- Levene's $p > .05$, so equal variances are reasonable and pooling would have been fine. We run Welch anyway: it is safe either way.

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Run the test

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
chocolate.R

```{r}
#| label: chocolate
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
# Welch (R's default): no equal-variance assumption
t.test(formula = concentration ~ group, data = choco)
```
:::

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Decision, effect size, and report

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Decide

$t(`r fdf(ch$df)`) = `r f2(ch$t)`$, $p$ `r fp(ch$p)`. Since $p < .05$, we **reject** $H_0$.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Effect size

$d = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p} = \dfrac{`r f2(ch$diff)`}{`r f2(ch$sp)`} = `r f2(ch$d)`$ (a **large** effect), where $s_p = \sqrt{s_p^2}$ is the square root of the pooled variance
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> An independent-samples t-test showed that students who ate chocolate (*M* = `r f2(ch$m1)`, *SD* = `r f2(ch$s1)`) scored significantly higher on the concentration task than students who did not (*M* = `r f2(ch$m2)`, *SD* = `r f2(ch$s2)`), [*`r apa_t(ch)`*]{.hl}, 95% CI [`r f2(ch$ci[1])`, `r f2(ch$ci[2])`], *d* = `r f2(ch$d)`.
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Design

> **Design Summary**\
> 40 students participated in a study examining how background music affects studying. Participants were randomly assigned to study a short academic text under one of two conditions: instrumental music or silence. After 15 minutes of study time, they completed a 10-item multiple-choice quiz.

- **IV:** study condition (instrumental music vs. silence)

- **DV:** quiz performance (number of correct answers out of 10)

- **Design:** between-subjects, randomized

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Hypotheses

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Null hypothesis $H_0$

Quiz performance is the same with music and in silence.

$\mu_\text{music} = \mu_\text{silence}$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Alternative hypothesis $H_A$

Quiz performance differs between the conditions.

$\mu_\text{music} \neq \mu_\text{silence}$
:::
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Data and results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: does-instrumental-music-improve-studying
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
group_plot(music, "group", "quiz_score", "Quiz score (out of 10)",
           "Music and study performance", kind = "violin")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: does-instrumental-music-improve-studying-2
#| echo: false
results_tbl(mu_)
```

Music: $M = `r f2(mu_$m1)`$, $SD = `r f2(mu_$s1)`$. Silence: $M = `r f2(mu_$m2)`$, $SD = `r f2(mu_$s2)`$.
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Run the test

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
music.R

```{r}
#| label: music
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
# Welch (R's default)
t.test(formula = quiz_score ~ group, data = music)
```
:::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Decision, effect size, and report

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Decide

$t(`r fdf(mu_$df)`) = `r f2(mu_$t)`$, $p$ `r fp(mu_$p)`. Since $p > .05$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Effect size

$d = \dfrac{`r f2(mu_$diff)`}{`r f2(mu_$sp)`} = `r f2(mu_$d)`$ (a **medium** effect)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> An independent-samples t-test showed that students who studied with music (*M* = `r f2(mu_$m1)`, *SD* = `r f2(mu_$s1)`) did not differ significantly on the quiz from students who studied in silence (*M* = `r f2(mu_$m2)`, *SD* = `r f2(mu_$s2)`), [*`r apa_t(mu_)`*]{.hl}, 95% CI [`r f2(mu_$ci[1])`, `r f2(mu_$ci[2])`], *d* = `r f2(mu_$d)`.
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Reading a non-significant result

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
A medium effect that is *not* significant is a hint that the study may have been too small to detect it. (If we had predicted a *direction* before collecting data, the one-tailed $p$ would be about `r f3(mu_$p / 2)`. But the direction has to be chosen **before** you see the result.)
:::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Design

> **Design Summary**\
> 80 students were randomly assigned to avoid phone use for 30 minutes before bed or to use their phones as normal. The next morning, all students rated their sleep quality on a 1-10 scale.

- **IV:** phone use before bed (yes vs. no)

- **DV:** sleep quality rating (1 = poor, 10 = excellent)

- **Design:** between-subjects, randomized

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Hypotheses

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Null hypothesis $H_0$

Sleep quality is the same with and without bedtime phone use.

$\mu_\text{no phone} = \mu_\text{phone}$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Alternative hypothesis $H_A$

Sleep quality differs between the conditions.

$\mu_\text{no phone} \neq \mu_\text{phone}$
:::
:::
:::::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Data and results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: does-bedtime-phone-use-affect-sleep
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
group_plot(sleep, "group", "sleep_quality", "Sleep quality (1-10)",
           "Phone use and sleep quality", kind = "bar")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: does-bedtime-phone-use-affect-sleep-2
#| echo: false
results_tbl(sl)
```

No phone: $M = `r f2(sl$m1)`$, $SD = `r f2(sl$s1)`$. Phone: $M = `r f2(sl$m2)`$, $SD = `r f2(sl$s2)`$.
:::
:::::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Run the test

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
sleep.R

```{r}
#| label: sleep
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
# Welch (R's default)
t.test(formula = sleep_quality ~ group, data = sleep)
```
:::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Decision, effect size, and report

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Decide

$t(`r fdf(sl$df)`) = `r f2(sl$t)`$, $p$ `r fp(sl$p)`. Since $p > .05$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$. The result is close, but not significant.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Effect size

$d = \dfrac{`r f2(sl$diff)`}{`r f2(sl$sp)`} = `r f2(sl$d)`$ (a **small-to-medium** effect)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> An independent-samples t-test showed that students who avoided their phones before bed (*M* = `r f2(sl$m1)`, *SD* = `r f2(sl$s1)`) did not differ significantly in sleep quality from students who used their phones (*M* = `r f2(sl$m2)`, *SD* = `r f2(sl$s2)`), [*`r apa_t(sl)`*]{.hl}, 95% CI [`r f2(sl$ci[1])`, `r f2(sl$ci[2])`], *d* = `r f2(sl$d)`.
:::
:::::

### Caffeine and alertness

> Does caffeine increase alertness? 40 participants were randomly assigned to caffeine or a placebo (`ex_3`: `Group`, `Alertness`; 20 per group). Alertness was scored on a 0-100 scale.

::: {.callout-tip .nonincremental}
## Your tasks

1.  State $H_0$ and $H_A$.
2.  Check the equal-variance assumption (Levene's Test).
3.  Run the independent-samples t-test, compute $d$, and write an APA sentence.
:::

## Practice

### Caffeine and alertness: data and answer

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
practice_3.R

```{r}
#| label: practice-3
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
set.seed(103)
ex_3 <- tibble(
  Group = factor(rep(c("Caffeine", "Placebo"), each = 20),
                 levels = c("Caffeine", "Placebo")),
  Alertness = c(rnorm(20, mean = 75, sd = 8), rnorm(20, mean = 68, sd = 8))
)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-important .nonincremental}
## Answer

$H_0: \mu_\text{caffeine} = \mu_\text{placebo}$; $H_A: \mu_\text{caffeine} \neq \mu_\text{placebo}$. Caffeine $M = `r f2(e3$m1)`$ vs. placebo $M = `r f2(e3$m2)`$: *`r apa_t(e3)`*, 95% CI [`r f2(e3$ci[1])`, `r f2(e3$ci[2])`], $d = `r f2(e3$d)`$.
:::
:::

## Terms to Know

### The vocabulary for this test

:::::: term-list
::: fragment
[Standard error of the difference]{.term-pill}

: How much the difference between two sample means bounces around from study to study. It is the denominator of $t$.
:::

::: fragment
[Pooled variance $s_p^2$]{.term-pill}

: A weighted average of the two group variances, used when the groups are assumed to share one population variance.
:::

::: fragment
[Welch's t-test]{.term-pill}

: An independent-samples $t$-test that lets each group keep its own variance. It is the default in `t.test()`.
:::

::: fragment
[Levene's test]{.term-pill}

: A test of $H_0$ that the group variances are equal.
:::
::::::

## Summary: Independent-Samples t-Test

- Compares **two independent groups**.

- Tests whether the difference in means is significant.

- **Welch's** t-test (R's default) does not assume equal variances. The **pooled** version needs them.

- Check assumptions: independence, normality, equal variance (look at the SDs, then Levene's Test, or just use Welch).

- Report the test, the means and SDs, the confidence interval, and an **effect size** ($d$).
